extracted.intended_audience: Researchers and scientists who serve as manuscript reviewers for peer-reviewed (primarily biomedical) journals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for scientists acting as peer reviewers of research manuscripts, focusing on ethical responsibilities, how to decide whether to review, how to handle and evaluate manuscripts, and how to write constructive reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the peer review process and the reviewer’s role
rubrics_metrics.description: To be a good reviewer, one must understand the peer review process and the role the reviewer is expected to play in that process (editors, editorial boards, staff, selection of reviewers, final decision-making).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should know how manuscripts are handled (editorial staff vs scientific editors), that reviewers are consultants to the journal, that reviews often have sections for editor-only and author-facing comments, and that reviewers' identities are known to editors though often not released to authors. Awareness of this structure should shape the content and tone of reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a good reviewer
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors look for reviewers with expertise in the subject matter who are objective, have good judgment, can think critically and logically, can write accurate/readable/helpful critiques, are reliable, and can meet deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expertise alone is insufficient. Good reviewers must be objective, timely, provide incisive scientific analysis, and produce reviews that are helpful to both editors and authors. Journals keep records of reviewer timeliness and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do you have the expertise the editor is looking for?
rubrics_metrics.description: Before agreeing to review, assess whether you understand the hypotheses, model systems, methods, analyses, and can judge data quality and significance for the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If in doubt, contact the editor to discuss. Recognize that multiple reviewers are selected to provide complementary expertise (e.g., clinician, lab scientist, statistician). Use review forms' comments-to-editor section to request additional reviews if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the work too close to your own?
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid reviewing manuscripts that overlap substantially with experiments you are performing, planning, or preparing for publication, because even ethical actions can create conflicts or perceptions of misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the manuscript overlaps with your work, contact the editor immediately and decline to review; ideally do so when you have seen only the title/abstract and avoid receiving the full manuscript. Return the manuscript if already received and discuss with the editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do you have any real or apparent conflicts of interest?
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential reviewers must assess whether real or apparent conflicts exist that could or could appear to compromise objectivity or the perceived value of the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards vary across journals; reviewers must evaluate whether a) their objectivity could be compromised, b) their objectivity could appear compromised, or c) their reputation could be at risk. When in doubt, disclose to and discuss with the editor and err on the side of caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional affiliations as conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors from your institution create potential conflicts; even if you do not know them personally, perceptions and possible pressures may compromise or appear to compromise objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decline to review papers from your own institution. Consider recent employment history, job negotiations, and institutional financial/research ties; these may create institutional conflicts of interest that should be disclosed or avoid reviewing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborators and recent co-authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers by present collaborators, mentors, or recent co-authors present ongoing conflicts of interest and should generally not be reviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ongoing collaborations usually require declining. For older, tenuous connections judge case-by-case. If unsure, disclose the relationship to the editor and request guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other personal relationships and seniority effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Close personal friends, family members, or authors you dislike; or senior influential authors, can create conflicts or discomfort that affect objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reviewing if personal relationships (positive or negative) could bias judgment or create perception issues. Decline diplomatically and inform the editor; be prepared to judge whether you could still be fair if you accept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Financial ties — employment by a company whose product is tested, consulting fees, large equity holdings, fiduciary roles, patents/licensing, funding from the company, provision of free reagents — can create significant conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the magnitude and relevance of financial ties. Some roles (company employee, large consulting payments, board membership, patent/licensing) generally preclude review; smaller or indirect ties (token honoraria, diversified mutual funds) may be acceptable but require disclosure per journal policy. Consider spouse/partner/dependent finances and institutional conflicts as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal beliefs may impair objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Strongly held personal or public positions (e.g., religious belief opposing evolution, vocal stances on controversial social issues) can bias or create the appearance of bias in reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If personal beliefs could compromise your ability to be objective, disclose to the editor and decline to review if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific conflicts of interest (competition/overlap)
rubrics_metrics.description: Active competition in a research area or work that is closely related to yours can create conflicts of interest that preclude or complicate reviewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If labs are competing or projects overlap, decline or discuss with the editor; journals must balance expertise and objectivity, and avoiding all such conflicts could also exclude necessary experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: When in doubt, discuss with the editor; err on side of caution
rubrics_metrics.description: There are often gray areas regarding conflicts and suitability; reviewers should consult editors when uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two prudent rules: 1) when in doubt, discuss the potential conflict with the editor; 2) when in doubt, err on the side of caution (i.e., decline if necessary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do you have the time to review within the requested time frame?
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should only accept manuscripts they can assess thoroughly within the journal's timeframe (often 48 hours to 2-3 weeks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most reviewers spend 1–2 hours for a typical review, more for difficult cases. It is unethical to accept if you cannot perform a thoughtful review in time; decline rather than provide a superficial critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscripts under review are confidential documents; handle accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts contain unpublished data and ideas that must be kept confidential; they should be stored securely and not shared, cited, or used for your own research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not share the paper or its contents; do not use ideas or data in your own work; destroy paper copies securely after the review; maintain confidentiality of the review's outcome until publication. Confidentiality violations betray authors and editors and undermine the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passing the manuscript to someone else requires permission
rubrics_metrics.description: You may not give the manuscript to a colleague for review unless the editor has explicitly permitted it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If permitted (or asked to suggest alternates), inform the editor who the actual reviewer is so records and web-access can be configured; disclose when a junior colleague assisted so they receive credit; editors rarely deny such requests but must be informed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contacting the author is generally not allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: Most journals regulate contact between reviewers and authors to preserve confidentiality and anonymity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need information from the authors, contact journal staff who will communicate on your behalf. Direct contact with authors should only occur after discussing it with the editor and obtaining permission in rare circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seeking help: permissible with caution and disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Asking a colleague anonymized, domain-specific questions may be acceptable, but broader consultation about the manuscript requires editor permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If permitted to consult someone, ensure the consultant understands confidentiality obligations; note in comments-to-editor that a colleague has seen the paper and assisted so the consultant gets appropriate recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: You are the agent of the journal, not the friend of the author
rubrics_metrics.description: The reviewer’s primary obligation is to advise the journal on suitability for publication, not to assist the author as a colleague or to avoid recommending rejection due to sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers must be willing to recommend rejection for flawed work and to challenge poor science even if uncomfortable. Avoid allowing collegial empathy to override the duty to uphold scientific standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus your review on scientific merit rather than mere editorial issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews should evaluate the science: importance and novelty, appropriateness of materials/methods/model systems, rigor of experimental design (including controls), quality of data, appropriateness of statistical analyses, rigor of interpretation, and validity of conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While point out editorial problems that obscure science (ambiguous wording, scientific misstatements, poor referencing), do not waste time correcting minor spelling/grammar. Cite specific figures, tables, or text sections to support criticisms; provide citations when relying on literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the paper’s appropriateness for the journal
rubrics_metrics.description: A reviewer should assess not only scientific quality but also suitability for the specific journal’s audience and standards (general-interest vs specialty journal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It may be appropriate to recommend that a high-quality paper be published elsewhere if it is mismatched to the journal. Note journal-specific standards or review-form questions about critical points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and raise ethical concerns in review (IRB, animal welfare, undisclosed conflicts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should check compliance with ethical standards for human subjects, animal welfare, and disclosure of funding or conflicts of interest, and raise these issues when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite the specific aspects causing concern and reference relevant guidelines/regulations. Report both in comments to the authors (if appropriate) and to the editor, since journals have explicit policies on these matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling suspected misconduct (duplication, plagiarism, fabrication, manipulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you suspect duplicate publication, plagiarism, data fabrication/falsification, or inappropriate manipulation, take careful, discreet steps before accusing authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain copies of the suspected original materials, carefully review the facts, then contact the editor in confidence with evidence. Both reviewer and editor should act discreetly, thorough, and thoughtfully due to potential career consequences for authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write reviews that are clear, concise, accurate, constructive, and supported
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews should advise the editor and guide authors: be clear, concise, accurate, and provide constructive suggestions supported by citations or references to specific parts of the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good reviews help authors improve design, execution, presentation, and interpretation. Criticisms should be accompanied by suggestions and references where appropriate. Reviews may be short for very good or very poor papers but must still be thoughtful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a collegial tone; avoid gratuitous rudeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Gratuitous rudeness, snide remarks, sarcasm, or obscene language are never appropriate and may be censored or withheld from authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase even serious scientific criticisms in a constructive and collegial manner—write as you would want a review for yourself or your most insecure trainee to be written. Reviewers set standards of collegiality in their field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-review confidentiality and record-keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: After submission, safely retain the review until receipt is confirmed and then destroy manuscript copies securely; confidentiality obligations continue after the review is completed and after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reveal identities of reviewers or internal review discussions even after publication. If discussing the paper later, reference the final published version rather than the confidential version you reviewed, since content may have changed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counter publication bias: be willing to recommend important negative results and thoughtful challenge to dogma
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize systematic publication bias toward positive or surprising findings; reviewers should be prepared to recommend publication of well-performed negative results and to thoughtfully assess papers that challenge dogma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat unexpected or paradigm-challenging papers with careful, objective scrutiny without dismissing them prematurely; encourage publication where scientifically justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remember anonymity is imperfect; avoid using anonymity as a cloak
rubrics_metrics.description: Although peer review is often blinded, reviewers can be identified by editors, and authors sometimes deduce reviewers from comments or writing style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use perceived anonymity as protection for rude or vindictive remarks. Provide constructive critiques and maintain professionalism in wording and tone.
